desc:
At minute 0 the node of a binary tree holding the value start catches an infection. In every following minute, each infected node infects all of its neighbours: its left child, its right child and its parent (when they exist).

Return the number of minutes after which the whole tree is infected. A tree with a single node needs 0 minutes.

How trees are given. There is no tree type here. A binary tree is passed as an integer array in level-order (top to bottom, left to right). A missing child is written as -1, and every real node value is non-negative. The children of a missing node are not listed, and trailing -1 entries are dropped, so a non-empty array never ends with -1. The empty tree is [].

For example, [1, 2, 3, -1, 4] describes the tree on the left: the root is 1 with children 2 and 3, node 2 has no left child and has 4 as its right child, and node 3 is a leaf.

    1
   / \
  2   3
   \
    4

For the tree below ([3, 5, 1, 6, 2, 0, 8, -1, -1, 7, 4]) and start = 2 the infection reaches 5, 7 and 4 after one minute, then 6 and 3, then 1, and finally 0 and 8, so the answer is 4. With start = 3 the answer is 3.

        3
      /   \
     5     1
    / \   / \
   6   2 0   8
      / \
     7   4
constraints: All node values are distinct, so a value identifies exactly one node
The array follows the encoding above exactly (valid level-order, no trailing -1)
hints: Each minute the infection moves exactly one edge. What is the answer in terms of distances?
The tree is infected completely when the farthest node from start is infected. That farthest distance is the answer.

Give every node a parent link (children are already known) and run a breadth-first search from start, counting levels; or compute the distance to every node by walking the array in level order after rooting the tree at start.
editorial: After t minutes exactly the nodes within distance t of the start are infected, so the answer is the largest distance from start to any node (its eccentricity).

Build the undirected neighbour lists (left, right, parent) in one pass and run a breadth-first search from the start; the number of BFS levels beyond the first is the answer. Each node and edge is processed once, so the solution is O(n).
